title: Disks, logs and the 3 am disk-full drill
part: Part 1 · The box, the way the gurus run it
brief: Full disks have four usual causes: a deleted file still open, inodes, a runaway log, and data that should never have lived on that filesystem. Model weights are the new fourth.
gurus: Thomas A. Limoncelli et al., The Practice of System and Network Administration

exercises.prompt: df -h / says 100% used, but du -xsh / adds up to 20 GB less. What is the most likely cause?
options: A deleted file that a running process still holds open, usually a log
exercises.explain: Deleting only removes the name; the blocks are freed when the last process closes the file. lsof +L1 lists open files with no links left. Restart the process, or truncate through /proc/<pid>/fd/<n>, to get the space back.

exercises.prompt: List files that are deleted but still held open by a process.
exercises.explain: +L1 selects files with a link count below 1, which is what a deleted-but-open file is.

exercises.prompt: `touch /var/tmp/x` fails with 'No space left on device', yet df -h shows 40% free. What do you check?
options: The disk is failing; replace it
Inodes, with df -i: millions of tiny files can use every inode before the blocks run out
exercises.explain: Every file needs an inode, and ext4 fixes the inode count when the filesystem is made. df -i shows it. A read-only mount fails with 'Read-only file system', not with no space.

exercises.prompt: Your inference box filled /var overnight. du -xh --max-depth=3 /var | sort -h ends with /var/lib/ollama/models at 180G. What is the fix?
options: rm -rf the biggest blob files by hand
Give model storage its own volume (OLLAMA_MODELS, HF_HOME), cap it, and remove unused models with the tool's own command (ollama rm, huggingface-cli delete-cache)
exercises.explain: Weights are tens of gigabytes each. Deleting blobs by hand breaks every model whose manifest still points at them; the tools know which layers are shared. On its own volume, a full model store cannot take down journald, apt and the database.

exercises.prompt: The logical volume vg0/var needs 50 GB more, and its filesystem must grow with it, online, in one command.
exercises.explain: -r (--resizefs) runs the filesystem resize after the LV grows, so you cannot forget it. ext4 and XFS both grow online.

exercises.prompt: This logrotate rule leaves the app unable to write after rotation. Rotate as the directory's owner, create the new file for appuser, and stop mixing create with copytruncate.
exercises.hint: Add `su appuser appuser`, change create to `create 0640 appuser appuser`, and drop copytruncate (the app reopens its log on every write, so create is enough). Dry-run on a real host with sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/chatty.
exercises.explain: With copytruncate, logrotate copies the log and truncates it in place, so `create` never runs: pick one. `su` makes logrotate rotate as the directory's owner, so rotated files keep the right owner and logrotate does not refuse a directory that a non-root group can write. Lab 5's VM 3 hides two more causes behind the same symptom: directory ownership and an SELinux label.

checks.name: rotates as the directory's owner (su appuser appuser)
new file is created for appuser to write
create and copytruncate are not both set (copytruncate makes create a no-op)
keeps a bounded number of old logs
